papers.title: Partial lesions of hypocretin neurons of the rat lateral hypothalamus affect wake and sleep regulation under increased sleep pressure
papers.abstract: Hypocretin(orexin)-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamic area are important for sleep and wake regulation in mammals and their damage in humans manifests clinically as narcolepsy. While in previous studies experimentally induced massive loss of these neurons revealed their physiological importance, small lesions and their manifestations can uncover more subtle features of sleep regulation and help understand the delicate processes in early stages of pathogenesis of narcolepsy. We studied the effects of partial lesions (approximately 30%) of hypocretin producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus on sleep patterns and EEG in rats. The lesions did not change the normal sleep and wake pattern in undisturbed rats. The effects of lesions manifested under increased sleep pressure after six hours of sleep deprivation, when they led to accelerated dynamics of compensatory slow wave sleep. The lesions also led to a slight decrease in theta frequency in wakefulness and in REM sleep, which we observed during undisturbed sleep and wake behavior as well as after sleep deprivation.

papers.title: Cross-Band Coupling of EEG Infraslow Oscillations during NREM Sleep in Mice.
papers.abstract: The infraslow oscillation (ISO) is a ~ 0.02 Hz rhythmic fluctuation in electroencephalographic (EEG) power during NREM sleep. Prior studies were limited to sigma-band ISO, linked to rhythmic norepinephrine release in mice. Whether ISOs exist in other bands, and how ISOs across bands are coupled, remain unknown. We analyzed cross-band ISO coupling across six frequency bands during NREM using a wild-type (WT) discovery dataset of 122 recordings from 72 mice and WT validation of 7 mice. A transgenic (TG) validation of 6 mice was added to test ISO coupling's robustness to Cre knock-in on the LepR gene (LepR-Cre). Band power time series were filtered to the ISO range of 0.01-0.03 Hz. Cross-band coupling was assessed using Spearman's correlation and phase-locking value (PLV) across all 15 band pairs. ISOs were strongest in alpha, sigma, beta, and theta bands, weak in gamma, and absent in delta. Alpha, sigma, beta, and theta ISOs formed a highly correlated motif with replication in WT and TG (r = 0.61-0.77), while gamma had moderate correlation (r = 0.30-0.42), and delta was uncorrelated (p > 0.05). All band pairs showed significant phase locking with replication (FDR-corrected q < 0.01), with stronger consistency in alpha, sigma, theta, and beta (PLV 0.54-0.71), and weaker consistency involving delta and gamma (PLV 0.12-0.37). EEG ISOs extend beyond the sigma band to alpha, beta, and theta bands, forming a strongly coupled motif that may reflect a fundamental organization principle of sleep microstructures at a minute scale.

ISOs were weak in gamma and absent in delta, suggesting a coupled minute-scale organization principle of sleep microstructures.

papers.title: A stochastic neural mass model for typical rhythms during sleep-wake transitions: Insights into dynamics driven by auditory noise.
papers.abstract: Sleep-wake transitions are essential for normal brain function. Although auditory noise can trigger sleep-wake transitions, how it influences the neural dynamics underlying these transitions and associated EEG rhythms remains unclear. Here, we propose a stochastic neural mass model to investigate how auditory noise modulates shifts in typical EEG rhythms during sleep-wake transitions. The model integrates the intrinsic sleep-wake regulatory circuit with rhythm-generating mechanisms and incorporates Gaussian colored noise (GCN) to represent auditory noise. Numerical simulations combined with deterministic and stochastic bifurcation-related analyses are used to evaluate how noise intensity, correlation rate, and intrinsic regulatory parameters influence transitions between alpha waves and slow oscillations. The model reproduces characteristic EEG rhythms during sleep and wakefulness, namely slow oscillations and alpha waves, and shows that the system exhibits a bistable regime in which slow oscillation and alpha wave limit cycles coexist as distinct attractors, with GCN inducing transitions between them. Increasing noise intensity and correlation rate bias the system toward the alpha waves associated with wakefulness, whereas lower values favor the slow oscillations associated with sleep. In addition, variations in intrinsic sleep-wake regulatory parameters reshape the basins of attraction of attractors, thereby modulating susceptibility to GCN-induced transitions. These results provide a model-based dynamical explanation for how auditory noise may modulate switching between typical EEG rhythm patterns associated with sleep-wake transitions and a reduced computational framework for investigating how auditory noise interacts with intrinsic neural regulation to influence sleep-wake rhythms. The framework may support future studies on sleep-wake regulation.

papers.title: Reduced-observable dynamic mode decomposition for identifying theta and beta activity in working-memory EEG
papers.abstract: The analysis of transient oscillatory activity in neural recordings remains challenging for linear methods, particularly when signals are nonlinear, noisy, and distributed across multiple channels. This paper introduces a Reduced-Observable Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (RO-eDMD) algorithm using a Random Fourier Features dictionary to characterize high-dimensional data in electroencephalography (EEG) recordings. The method extends the Koopman operator framework by incorporating rank reduction directly in the observable space and employing a randomized feature map that approximates the Gaussian kernel, enabling the capture of transient components without explicit dictionary optimization. To assess the method and demonstrate applicability, a logistic regression model is trained using a working memory paradigm as a test case, using dominant power values extracted via RO-eDMD in the theta band as a predictor and the type of event (encoding vs.\ fixation) as the dependent variable. We find correlations between oscillatory power and memory encoding events in the analyzed bands. Additionally, we find an increase in correlation associated with theta power and memory load, replicating similar results in the literature. The presented algorithm offers a computationally efficient, interpretable framework applied to a working memory paradigm dataset, but is relevant to the analysis of neural time series from diverse experimental contexts.

papers.title: Development of Circadian Circuitry Underlying Feeding-Fasting Rhythms in Drosophila Larvae
papers.abstract: Many organisms do not exhibit strong daily behavioral rhythms early in life. The consolidation of sleep and feeding to specific times of the day does not emerge until later in development. Disruptions to circadian behaviors in early life can lead to dysregulation of both neural development and metabolic homeostasis. However, the circuit mechanisms regulating feeding rhythm development are unknown. Here, we characterize the neural circuitry responsible for driving the development of feeding-fasting rhythms in early 3rd instar (L3) Drosophila larvae. We find that inactivation of both larval s-LNv circadian pacemaker neurons and SIFamide (SIFa) neurons in the pars intercerebralis disrupts feeding rhythm development. Additionally, our data indicate feeding rhythms likely emerge due to circuit connections forming between s-LNvs and SIFa neurons at the L3 stage. Finally, we show that reductions in signaling between s-LNv and SIFa neurons interfere with normal behavioral rhythm development in L3. Specifically, RNA interference-induced reductions in pigment-dispersing factor (pdf) signaling and SIFa signaling disrupt diurnal differences in both feeding and sleep, resulting in a loss of behavioral rhythms. Altogether, our findings identify for the first time the clock and clock output circuitry responsible for feeding rhythm regulation in developing organisms.

papers.title: Advancing Pediatric Sleep Assessment through Spectral Sleep Scoring: A Comparison with Polysomnography.
papers.abstract: Understanding how sleep changes across development requires methods that are both efficient and sensitive to maturational differences in sleep physiology. Spectral sleep scoring is a promising approach, but has primarily been validated in adult populations. This study presents and validates a spectral scoring approach for pediatric sleep. Participants (n = 192; 9-18y) completed overnight in-lab sleep studies. Visual scoring was determined by registered polysomnographic technologists and confirmed by board certified sleep physicians following AASM guidelines. Visual stages included: wake, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) stage 1 (N1), NREM stage 2 (N2), NREM stage 3 (N3), and rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep. Spectral activity within each epoch was assessed for the following spectral stages: Wake (40-95 Hz), Light (~11- 15.5 Hz), Hi Deep (1-3 Hz), Lo Deep (0.1-1 Hz), and REM (~17-26 Hz). Concordance rates were checked across agreement matrices between visual and spectral stages, with expected high agreement between: 1) visual Wake and spectral Wake; 2) visual N2 and spectral Light; 3) visual N3 and spectral HiDeep/LoDeep; and 4) visual REM and spectral REM. Cohen's κ was calculated from concordance matrices. There was high agreement between visual and spectral stages (71-89%, κ=.76). Our results provide evidence that spectral scoring is a promising method for efficiently scoring pediatric sleep. Moreover, this method provides additional, clinically relevant information that is not readily captured through traditional visual scoring. This may be particularly valuable for assessing sleep physiology in pediatric clinical populations, where developmental differences in EEG patterns may complicate visual scoring.

papers.title: NREM sleep microarchitecture is associated with internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning in early adolescence.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common in youth with anxiety disorders, yet most prior work relies on subjective measures and does not capture underlying neural processes. We examined whether alterations in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep oscillations are present in children with anxiety disorders and whether these features relate to internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning. Children aged 9-13 years with diagnosed anxiety disorders (ANX; n = 17) and typically developing non-psychiatric comparison participants (NC; n = 26) completed overnight polysomnography. Slow oscillations (SO) and slow and fast sleep spindles were characterized using validated automated detection algorithms. Participants also completed a pre-sleep emotional processing task, and parents provided standardized measures of youth mental health. Group differences and dimensional associations between NREM oscillations, internalizing symptoms, and behavioral indices of emotional processing were examined. Sleep architecture did not differ between groups. Slow spindle duration was shorter in the ANX group. Across the full sample, shorter slow spindle duration was associated with greater internalizing symptoms, whereas higher SO density was positively associated with internalizing symptoms. Children in the ANX group exhibited greater facial emotional arousal and more frequent look-away behavior during the emotional processing task. Across participants, greater emotional arousal and look-away behavior were associated with shorter spindle duration during subsequent sleep. Specific features of NREM microarchitecture were associated with individual differences in internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning during early adolescence. These findings highlight the potential relevance of NREM oscillations for understanding developmental links between sleep and youth psychopathology. Sleep disturbances are common in youth with anxiety disorders, yet most research has relied on subjective reports and broad measures of sleep quality. This study demonstrates that specific features of non-rapid eye movement sleep microarchitecture, particularly sleep spindle duration, are associated with anxiety, depression, and emotional responding during early adolescence even in the absence of differences in overall sleep quality or sleep stage distribution. These findings highlight the importance of examining neural features of sleep when investigating emotional functioning and internalizing psychopathology during development. More broadly, the results suggest that adolescence may represent a sensitive developmental window during which alterations in sleep physiology are linked to emotional functioning. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine how these sleep features relate to developmental trajectories of youth psychopathology.

papers.title: Photic Phase Shifts of the Mouse Circadian Clock Are Defined by Scene Irradiance Across Differences in the Spatial Distribution of Light.
papers.abstract: Light resets the mammalian circadian clock, but whether this response is determined solely by integrated light intensity (irradiance) or is also influenced by the spatial distribution of light remains unclear. We tested whether high-contrast or low-spatial-frequency patterns modulate circadian responses in mice independently of scene irradiance. Circadian phase shifts were measured following exposure to spatially patterned illumination, including high-contrast checkerboards and spot stimuli positioned at the horizon or zenith. Across all experiments, redistributing light within the visual field did not measurably alter phase-shift amplitude when irradiance was matched between paired conditions. Circadian responses were well predicted by total scene irradiance whereas a metric based on the region of highest radiance provided a poorer account of the data. These findings are consistent with effective spatial integration of light by the mouse circadian system. Within the range of spatial and irradiance conditions tested, our results support irradiance as a simple and effective metric for predicting circadian responses across light environments with divergent spatial distributions.

papers.title: Using wearable EEG to examine age trends in sleep macro- and micro-architecture across adolescence.
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a period of distinct maturational changes in sleep physiology. Age-related trends in sleep physiology have been captured using laboratory-based polysomnography, a method limited by logistical burden and high cost. We tested the ability of the Dreem3 sleep EEG headband to replicate established age effects in sleep physiology from late childhood through early adulthood. Typically developing youth (N = 100, 9-26 years) completed 3-4 consecutive nights of at-home sleep recording. We estimated age-related trends across eight macro-architecture and 15 micro-architecture variables with known age effects, and conducted exploratory analyses of 24 additional variables. Dreem3 replicated established age trends, including increases in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) stage 2%, and decreases in N3%, time in bed, NREM delta and theta power with increasing age. Exploratory analysis revealed age effects in twelve additional variables, including decreases in spindle activity with increasing age. Sleep EEG wearables offer an accessible way to characterize sleep physiology development.

papers.title: Modifiable glymphatic-related brain clearance physiology in humans: a critical narrative review of interventional evidence.
papers.abstract: The glymphatic model proposes that cerebrospinal fluid exchanges with interstitial fluid along perivascular pathways, potentially facilitating brain solute clearance. Interest in whether this physiology can be modified has prompted human studies of sleep, exercise, respiratory manipulation, circadian interventions, and neuromodulation, but these studies use endpoints that differ substantially in biological directness. This critical narrative review evaluates human interventional and longitudinal evidence for modifiable glymphatic-related brain-clearance physiology and distinguishes altered neurofluid dynamics from evidence of solute transport. Sleep provides the most convincing convergent evidence: total sleep deprivation impairs intrathecal tracer clearance, whereas normal sleep increases the overnight appearance of amyloid-β and tau in plasma. Sustained aerobic exercise modifies contrast-based brain influx and meningeal lymphatic measures, although evidence remains preliminary. Slow deep breathing and intermittent hypercapnia alter cerebrospinal fluid dynamics; hypercapnia also increases several plasma brain-protein concentrations, but enhanced clearance is unconfirmed. Bright light therapy and transcranial magnetic stimulation modify diffusion-based perivascular imaging proxies that remain indirect and biologically nonspecific. Human neurofluid physiology may therefore be modifiable, but changes in fluid motion or surrogate imaging signals should not be equated with enhanced solute clearance. Clinically meaningful modulation will require controlled studies linking mechanistic target engagement to direct solute transport and neurological outcomes.

papers.title: REM sleep infraslow rhythms correlate with neuropsychiatric symptom severity.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is commonly divided into phasic and tonic substates based on higher and lower oculomotor activity, respectively. Our previous study described an alternative framework in which REM temporal structure forms a continuum of infraslow rhythms (∼0.01 Hz) across brain and body physiology. We now ask whether these infraslow rhythms vary with neuropsychiatric symptoms, given the long-standing but still inconsistent links between REM and mood- or trauma-related disorders. Using a cross-sectional polysomnographic dataset from male veterans, we examined 59 participants for correlations between REM infraslow rhythms and neuropsychiatric symptom scores, excluding participants with moderate/severe apnea. Oscillations in REM respiratory rate, but not cardiac rate or electroencephalogram beta power, showed higher infraslow frequencies in participants with multiple symptoms, including posttraumatic stress, pain, anxiety, depression, and cognitive difficulties. No significant correlations were found between these symptoms and conventional REM metrics (e.g., REM density, latency and duration). To further examine REM beyond phasic/tonic binarization, we analyzed the timing between oculomotor activity and infraslow oscillations. Eye movements occurred preferentially during periods of high respiratory rate, low beta power and intermediate cardiac rate, with no changes in these temporal relationships across symptom severity. Neuropsychiatric associations with REM infraslow rhythms spanned multiple symptom domains but were physiologically specific, with respiratory rate oscillations representing the strongest readout of symptom burden. Furthermore, REM infraslow cycles across brain and body were differentially aligned with eye movements: a temporal pattern that may serve as a physiological target for neuropsychiatric and mechanistic research. Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep has long been studied in relation to neuropsychiatric conditions, but traditional measures of the timing and duration of REM episodes have shown limited consistency for symptom tracking. This study addresses this gap by highlighting a less explored physiological feature within REM episodes: minute-scale, or infraslow, rhythms in respiratory and cardiac rate, as well as oculomotor and brain activity. We report that REM infraslow oscillations, particularly in respiratory rate, occur at higher frequency in participants with worse trauma/mood symptoms and cognitive difficulties. This work is evidence of a possible new REM sleep-based biomarker for multiple diseases.

papers.title: Stability of the Epileptogenic Index across seizures and the effects of sleep and withdrawal of anti-seizure medications.
papers.abstract: Epileptogenic Index (EI) is a promising index to evaluate the epileptogenicity of the brain tissue and is useful in planning epilepsy surgery. We aimed to evaluate whether EI maps are consistent across seizures within patients and whether EI-derived measures are affected by the vigilance state and anti-seizure medication (ASM) dose. We analyzed 127 stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) seizures from 19 patients. EI was calculated in all seizures. Within-patient EI consistency was assessed using pairwise Spearman correlations between seizure-specific EI maps. To assess the effects of vigilance and ASM on EI consistency, we calculated a contact-level p_weighted EI score that combines the frequency of suprathreshold EI involvement and mean EI magnitude, separately across vigilance states and in a subset of patients with different ASM states. Mean seizure-to-seizure EI correlations ranged from 0.11 to 0.81, indicating substantial variability in within-patient EI consistency. Seven patients showed high consistency (≥0.6) and four showed low consistency (≤0.3). At the contact level, no differences in p_weighted EI were found between wakefulness and sleep. In contrast, p_weighted EI was significantly higher during reduced ASM compared with full ASM doses. EI maps are not uniformly stable across seizures. ASM reduction may broaden or intensify EI-defined epileptogenic involvement, suggesting that ASM status should be considered when interpreting EI during SEEG evaluation. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation to determine their clinical utility for surgical planning. The Epileptogenic Index (EI) measures the involvement of a recorded brain area during a specific seizure. This study shows that EI patterns can vary significantly between different seizures in the same patient. While sleep states do not change these patterns, reducing a patient's anti-seizure medications increases EI values, making seizures appear to spread more broadly. These medication-induced changes must be carefully considered to accurately map the epileptic network for surgical decisions.

papers.title: Sleep and the Gut-Brain Axis: Bidirectional, Converging Mechanisms Linking Brain Health, Neuroinflammation, and Neurodegeneration.
papers.abstract: Sleep and the gastrointestinal (GI) tract interact in a complex and reciprocal relationship, although the molecular and physiological pathways underlying this interaction remain only partially defined. Communication between the central (CNS) and enteric nervous systems (ENS) spans neural, immune, endocrine, and metabolic pathways, including vagal nerve signaling, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, gut-resident microbiota, and circulating microbial metabolites, such as bile acids with neuroinflammatory or neurotransmitter activity. In this narrative review, we synthesize evidence from animal models, observational cohorts, and intervention trials to map this bidirectional axis, focusing on several underexamined modulatory mechanisms including the interaction between the gut microbiome and the glymphatic system, the brain's perivascular waste-clearance network, which is implicated in the removal of amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau in Alzheimer's disease; neuroendocrine regulation and sex-related differences in gut microbiome composition and sleep patterns, which may help explain the divergent neurodegenerative disease risks between men and women; and age-related parallel trajectories of microbiome senescence and sleep fragmentation in older adults. We discuss melatonin, cortisol, estrogen, and ghrelin as endocrine mediators linking circadian biology to gut physiology, and we consider how environmental and lifestyle factors further perturb this system. These mechanisms form an integrative framework of the gut-brain-sleep axis and highlight priority directions for mechanistic and translational research, including significant nodes in this pathway where targeted interventions may help cognitive resilience and slow the neurodegenerative disease progression. More research clarifying these mechanisms may help identify the most promising targets, potentially leading to personalized, precision-medicine-based therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: The Sleep-Wake Classification Performance of Pediatric-Trained Machine Learning Algorithms for Raw Accelerometer Data.
papers.abstract: Actigraphy sleep-wake classification methods increasingly seek to leverage raw acceleration data and machine-learning-based classification, but performance evaluation in pediatrics is limited. We trained machine-learning models using pediatric data and compared their sleep-wake classification performance with existing algorithms for children. Sixty-five children (46% female, ages 5.3-17.7 years) completed in-lab overnight polysomnography and wore a GENEActiv device on their non-dominant wrist. The acceleration data were converted into 30-second epochs and aligned with physician-scored sleep-wake data from electroencephalography. Eight machine-learning models were trained using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Epoch-by-epoch analyses generated performance metrics (e.g., balanced accuracy [BA]) and discrepancy analyses provided overall sleep duration bias estimates. The combination of highest performance and least bias was used to rank using Euclidean distance scores - where a lower score represents closer to perfect performance and zero bias. For benchmarking, we included GGIR sleep scoring algorithms and an adult trained random forest classifier. Overall, 560.1 hours of polysomnography and actigraphy data were collected (74.4% of epochs were scored as sleep). The pediatric-trained local-global long-short term memory (LSTM) classifier had the most optimal epoch-by-epoch performance (e.g., BA=0.85, sensitivity=0.88, specificity=0.83, ROC-AUC=0.95, and Cohen's kappa=0.67). These metrics exceeded that of an adult-trained random forest classifier and GGIR-based algorithms. Discrepancy analyses revealed that overall sleep duration was underestimated by an average of 25 minutes using the LSTM classifier with no proportional bias. We trained eight pediatric sleep-wake classifiers that had a strong ability to detect sleep and wake, with the LSTM classifier being most optimal.

papers.title: Mechanisms of auditory cortex injury and the protective effects of reoxygenation in a rat model of intermittent hypoxia.
papers.abstract: Intermittent hypoxia associated with obstructive sleep apnea can impair auditory function, but the early mechanisms underlying auditory cortical injury and the extent to which these changes recover after the restoration of normoxia remain unclear. This study investigated the mechanisms underlying auditory cortical injury in a rat model of intermittent hypoxia and evaluated the protective effects of reoxygenation. Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats were assigned to control, intermittent hypoxia, intermittent hypoxia followed by 1 week of normoxic recovery, or control followed by normoxic recovery groups. Short-term intermittent hypoxia caused high-frequency hearing loss and increased spontaneous firing in the primary auditory cortex. After 1 week of normoxic recovery, auditory thresholds and cortical firing rates returned to levels comparable to those in the control group. Glutamate levels did not differ significantly among the groups, whereas γ-aminobutyric acid and 5-hydroxytryptamine levels were elevated in the intermittent hypoxia followed by normoxic recovery group. Intermittent hypoxia increased superoxide dismutase activity, reduced catalase activity, and elevated the levels of tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, and interleukin-6. Normoxic recovery normalized catalase activity and reduced tumor necrosis factor-α and interleukin-6 levels, whereas superoxide dismutase activity and interleukin- 1β levels remained elevated. Metabolomic analysis identified alterations in unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis, branched-chain amino acid metabolism, ferroptosis-related pathways, redox-related metabolism, and amino acid and protein turnover, several of which persisted after recovery. These findings indicate that acute intermittent hypoxia-induced auditory dysfunction and cortical hyperexcitability are reversible, whereas redox, inflammatory, and metabolic abnormalities recover asynchronously. Persistent molecular disturbances after functional recovery may provide potential targets for further investigation of obstructive sleep apnea-associated central auditory injury.

papers.title: Effect of circadian-oriented goal-directed sedation on sleep quality and clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption and circadian rhythm disturbances are common in mechanically ventilated intensive care unit (ICU) patients and are associated with delirium, prolonged ventilation, and poor clinical outcomes. Conventional sedation strategies may further impair sleep architecture and circadian regulation. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effects of circadian-oriented, goal-directed sedation on sleep quality and clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. This study enrolled 65 mechanically ventilated patients admitted to ICU at Suzhou Ninth People's Hospital between March 2024 and December 2024. Using convenience sampling, 33 patients admitted between March and July 2024 were allocated to the control group and received routine sedation and nursing care, while 32 patients admitted between August and December 2024 were formed the intervention group and received sedation management individualized according to circadian sleep-wake patterns. Sleep quality was assessed on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 after intervention using the Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire (RCSQ) and a portable sleep monitor. Delirium was evaluated by Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU). Sedative dosage, duration of mechanical ventilation, length of ICU and hospital stay, , clinical improvement rate, complications, and hospitalization costs were compared between groups. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the two groups. Sleep quality improved over time in both groups; however, Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire scores were significantly higher in the intervention group at all assessment points (p < 0.05). Patients receiving circadian-oriented sedation experienced shorter durations of mechanical ventilation, reduced ICU and total hospital stays, higher rates of clinical improvement, and lower hospitalization costs compared with the control group (p < 0.05). The incidence of complications, including delirium, was also significantly lower in the intervention group. Sedation management aligned with circadian sleep-wake patterns significantly improves sleep quality, reduces sedative requirements, lowers delirium incidence, and shortens mechanical ventilation duration, demonstrating a favorable safety profile in mechanically ventilated patients.

papers.title: Tegmental atrophy in isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder: ex vivo MRI-informed in vivo imaging.
papers.abstract: Isolated rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder (iRBD) is an early-stage synucleinopathy characterized by brainstem pathology. In rodents, the pontine tegmentum contains a REM sleep centre, the sublaterodorsal nucleus, which expresses corticotropin-releasing hormone binding protein (CRHBP). While the involvement of brainstem pathophysiology is thus implicated in iRBD, its solid evidence remains scarce in humans due to the difficulty in identifying small brainstem nuclei with conventional MRI technology alone. Here, we aimed to detect tegmental atrophy in iRBD with voxel-based morphometry (VBM) analysis combined with a novel human brainstem atlas. Structural MRIs from 98 patients with iRBD and 114 controls were analysed to investigate grey matter volume using VBM. Our unique approach involved detailed assessments of the VBM results, guided by a high-resolution MRI-based atlas of the human brainstem. This brainstem atlas was founded on ex vivo MRI of 10 post-mortem human specimens. We validated it with CRHBP immunostaining, which aided in identifying putative REM sleep-regulating nuclei in humans. We applied this brainstem atlas to identify atrophy in specific brainstem regions in iRBD and correlate their volumes with clinical and polysomnographic measures. Voxel-based morphometry revealed a focal cluster of grey matter atrophy in the dorsal pontine tegmentum of iRBD patients, including the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus, ventral part (LDTgV) and the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PTg). Our atlas-based analysis confirmed the LDTgV as the site of most conspicuous atrophy, revealing a significant volume reduction in iRBD patients compared with controls with a moderate effect size (Cohen's d = 0.44, Bonferroni-corrected P = 0.019). Furthermore, greater atrophy in the LDTgV and the PTg was associated with more severe autonomic dysfunction as measured by Scales for Outcomes in Parkinson's Disease-Autonomic dysfunction scores (partial r = -0.237, P = 0.021 and partial r = -0.236, P = 0.021, respectively). In 23 patients from whom quantitative polysomnographic data were available, LDTgV atrophy was correlated with the percentage ratio of REM sleep without atonia (partial r = -0.491, P = 0.028). Histological analysis confirmed that the LDTgV is selectively enriched with CRHBP-positive neurons, a putative marker for REM sleep-on neurons. We provided novel evidence for the involvement of LDTgV, the putative human homologue of the murine sublaterodorsal nucleus, in iRBD. The present findings advance our understanding of the neuroanatomical basis of iRBD and will contribute to the development of early biomarkers for α-synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Everyday discrimination alters cognitive benefits of restorative non-rapid eye movement sleep in Black adults.
papers.abstract: Restorative non-rapid eye movement sleep has been linked to cognitive functioning. Yet, it remains unclear whether experiences of discrimination, a persistent form of identity-based adversity, shape how objectively measured restorative non-rapid eye movement sleep relates to cognitive outcomes in Black Americans. Ninety-two Black adults completed the Everyday Discrimination Scale, a cognitive assessment, and three nights of at-home sleep monitoring. Restorative non-rapid eye movement sleep was indexed using N2-N3 delta power. Moderation analyses evaluated whether everyday discrimination altered the association between restorative non-rapid eye movement sleep and global cognition, assessed with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, as well as visuospatial memory, assessed with the Benson Complex Figure task, adjusting for age, sex, marital status, education, subjective socioeconomic status, body mass index, and sleep efficiency. Discrimination moderated the relationship between restorative non-rapid eye movement sleep and global cognition. At lower levels of discrimination, greater levels of restorative non-rapid eye movement sleep corresponded to higher global cognition scores, whereas at higher levels of discrimination, a greater level of restorative non-rapid eye movement sleep corresponded to lower global cognition scores. The interaction between restorative non-rapid eye movement sleep and discrimination on visuospatial memory was not significant after full covariate adjustment, with education emerging as a significant independent predictor of visuospatial memory. The findings suggest that associations between restorative non-rapid eye movement sleep and global cognition vary across levels of everyday discrimination among Black adults, independent of socioeconomic and health-related factors. These results highlight discrimination as a relevant contextual factor to consider when examining sleep-cognition relationships in cognitive aging.

papers.title: Sleep deprivation disrupts error awareness and subsequent behavioural regulation.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation is known to impair cognitive performance, yet its effects on error awareness and subsequent behavioural adjustments remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated how sleep loss affects the use of subjective performance evaluation to guide post-error adaptations. Thirty healthy adults completed a novel, gamified error awareness multi-rule Simon task once while well rested and once after one night of total sleep deprivation. On each trial, participants reported both their task response and subjective evaluation of response accuracy. This design allowed us to dissociate objective performance from subjective error awareness and to examine their influence on subsequent behaviour over time. Sleep deprivation slowed responses, reduced accuracy, increased missed responses, and decreased the proportion of consciously detected errors, with impairments increasing over time on task. Both objective errors and subjective error judgements were associated with subsequent slowing. When well rested, subjective-error-associated slowing exceeded objective-error-associated slowing. This difference was reduced under sleep deprivation. Specifically, objectively correct responses judged as errors were followed by slowing relative to correctly judged correct responses, and this slowing was attenuated under sleep deprivation. Accuracy showed post-error decreases that were most pronounced following objective errors. Together, the findings indicate that sleep deprivation reduces error awareness and is associated with altered post-error behavioural regulation.

papers.title: Muscular Response in Sleep-Disordered Breathing Patients: New Methods of Assessment and Measurement.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a heterogeneous disorder influenced by both anatomical collapsibility and non-anatomical factors, such as neuromuscular response. Identifying these traits through simplified clinical surrogates is crucial for personalized precision medicine. This exploratory retrospective study evaluated 207 home polygraphy recordings of Italian patients to assess sleep-stage-specific Apnea-Hypopnea Index (REM vs. NREM AHI) as a clinical surrogate indicator of the balance between anatomical collapsibility and neuromuscular compensation. Patients were stratified by severity into simple snorers (AHI < 5 events/h), mild OSA (AHI 5-15 events/h), and severe OSA (AHI > 30 events/h). REM and NREM AHI values were compared and correlated with Apnea Index (AI), Hypopnea Index (HI), body mass index (BMI), and cumulative nocturnal desaturation indices (CT < 90% and T < 90 min). In non-severe patients (simple snorers and mild OSA), REM AHI was significantly higher than NREM AHI (REM/NREM ratio > 1), suggesting relative neuromuscular protection during NREM sleep. Conversely, in severe OSA patients, the REM/NREM ratio progressively decreased and approached unity, with NREM AHI prevailing. Furthermore, NREM predominance was significantly associated with a higher AI and a worse cumulative desaturation indicating a globally more severe disease. A predominance of REM AHI characterizes milder OSA presentations with effective NREM muscular compensation, whereas NREM predominance aligns with an anatomically dominant, severe phenotype. Decomposing AHI into REM and NREM components provides a practical, readily available clinical surrogate to estimate the anatomy-neuromuscular balance and guide PALM-oriented personalized treatments.

papers.title: Integrated assessment of driving performance, eye movements, and cognitive function in obstructive sleep apnea: A pilot study.
papers.abstract: Motor vehicle accident (MVA) risk is greater in patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), yet the functional domains most closely linked to driving-related impairment remain incompletely understood. This exploratory pilot study aimed to perform an integrated assessment of driving performance, eye movements, vigilance, and cognitive function in OSA and to examine their relationships with disease severity and treatment response. Adult drivers with suspected OSA underwent assessment using a driving simulator, Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT), eye-tracking, and the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB). Participants with moderate-to-severe OSA (apnea-hypopnea index ≥20) who initiated continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy underwent re-evaluation after 6-12 months. At baseline, single-task reaction time in the driving simulator was positively correlated with apnea severity. In contrast, response accuracy under multitask plus steering conditions was associated with nocturnal hypoxemia (T90), suggesting differential contributions of apnea frequency and oxygen desaturation to driving performance. Eye-tracking parameters, including saccade amplitude and fixation duration, were significantly correlated with both driving performance and spatial working memory error scores. Following CPAP therapy, simple reaction times improved in both the driving simulator and PVT, whereas changes in multitasking performance and CANTAB measures were not statistically significant. Basic psychomotor speed was associated with OSA severity and improved following CPAP therapy, suggesting within-subject improvement of vigilance-dependent processes. In contrast, integrated oculomotor and executive function measures were more closely linked to complex driving performance, indicating that multidomain assessment may better characterize driving-related impairment in OSA. These findings provide preliminary evidence to guide future hypothesis-driven studies.

papers.title: Rapid phase resetting of Aedes aegypti circadian rhythms by transient alterations in light exposure.
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks enable mosquitoes to anticipate recurring environmental variations and coordinate behaviors critical for survival and disease transmission, such as locomotion, reproduction, host-seeking, and blood-feeding, with times of day when performance is maximal. In Aedes aegypti , locomotor activity follows a robust diurnal rhythm shaped by endogenous circadian clocks and environmental cues, among which light has been shown to be the primary source of temporal information. While early studies established the role of light in regulating locomotor activity, behavior, oviposition and pupation, it remains unclear which features of a light cycle drive changes in circadian rhythms. This question is increasingly relevant as Ae. aegypti is frequently exposed to artificial and dynamic lighting conditions in urban environments. Here, we investigated how transient changes in light schedules influence circadian rhythms in locomotor activity by systematically manipulating the timing, duration, and direction of light exposure. Using a high-throughput assay, we tested over 1900 individuals, including wild-type and timeless knockout mutants, and showed that a single day of altered lighting is sufficient to induce robust phase shifts, with no evidence of masking effects. A 6-hour light pulse was sufficient to re-entrain mosquitoes regardless of the timing of the pulse, and phase shifts were primarily driven by the offset time of the light pulse, indicating that light-offset acts as a major zeitgeber . Together, these findings challenge conventional assumptions about the timescale of circadian synchronization and highlight the remarkable plasticity of mosquito behavior in response to anthropogenic light. Eventually, these effects could explain the rapid adaptation of the species to urban environments and have potential consequences for disease transmission dynamics. A single day of changes in the light schedule is sufficient to reset the phase of Aedes aegypti 's circadian clock. Circadian phase resetting requires at least four to six hours of light exposure.Advancing the circadian phase is easier than delaying it.

papers.title: Modified sleep stage sequence analysis based on the stage immediately preceding each REM sleep period during nocturnal polysomnography to identify candidates for narcolepsy workup.
papers.abstract: To evaluate whether a modified sleep stage sequence (SSS) method based on a single epoch immediately preceding each rapid eye movement (REM) sleep period during nocturnal polysomnography (nPSG) could help identify candidates for further narcolepsy workup. This study retrospectively analyzed 204 participants: 39 with narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), 63 with narcolepsy type 2 (NT2), 62 with idiopathic hypersomnia (IH), and 40 healthy controls (HC). In nPSG, REM periods were classified by the single 30-s epoch immediately preceding their onset, excluding sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs). The participant-level SSS(W/N1) ratio was the proportion of remaining REM periods preceded by wakefulness or N1. Decision trees distinguished NT1/NT2 from IH/HC using REM sleep latency (REML) alone or with this ratio, with 50 stratified 70/30 hold-out splits for internal validation. In pooled multiple sleep latency test SOREMPs, the proposed method showed the same between-group ordering as conventional SSS. In pooled nocturnal REM periods excluding SOREMPs, the frequency of SSS(W/N1) was highest in NT1 and showed a stepwise numerical gradient across NT1, NT2, IH, and HC. Adding the SSS(W/N1) ratio to REML increased the median validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.64 [interquartile range, 0.63-0.67] to 0.70 [0.68-0.74]. Two rounded high-specificity rules were derived: Rule A (REML-based), REML < 40 min; and Rule B (SSS-enhanced), SSS(W/N1) ratio ≥ 0.4 with REML < 125 min. Median sensitivity/specificity were 23%/98% and 37%/97%, respectively. A modified pre-REM SSS measure derived from routine nPSG may help prioritize patients for further narcolepsy workup.

papers.title: Mindfulness-based perioperative care, sleep architecture, autonomic regulation, and early atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence after radiofrequency catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation: a prospective observational cohort study.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to examine the relationship between perioperative care by mindfulness and sleep quality, autonomic regulation, inflammatory activity, and early recurrence of atrial tachyarrhythmia (AT) following radiofrequency catheter ablation (RFCA) for atrial fibrillation (AF). This was a prospective assessor-blinded observational cohort study involving 124 patients with AF who underwent their initial radiofrequency catheter ablation from April 2023 to December 2025. Conventional perioperative care was provided to one group (n=62), while the other group (n=62) received mindfulness-based perioperative care. To reduce baseline imbalance, propensity score overlap weighting was implemented. Objective sleep architecture was assessed by overnight polysomnography and autonomic function was examined by HRV analysis. hs-CRP, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β, and MCP-1 were analyzed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Health related quality of life was determined based on the SF-36 questionnaire. Compared with conventional care, mindfulness-based perioperative care was associated with greater observed changes in total sleep time (389.4 ± 43.8 vs. 365.7 ± 45.2 min, P=0.012), sleep efficiency (77.4 ± 7.2% vs. 71.2 ± 7.8%, P=0.004), sleep onset latency (27.1 ± 8.8 vs. 34.8 ± 10.5 min, P=0.009), and PSQI scores (7.2 ± 2.5 vs. 9.3 ± 2.9, P=0.006). The mindfulness group also showed lower inflammatory biomarker levels and differences in short-term autonomic indices, including a lower LF/HF ratio (1.39 ± 0.41 vs. 1.66 ± 0.54, P=0.005). Early atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence occurred in 6 patients (9.7%) in the mindfulness-based perioperative care group and in 11 patients (17.7%) in the conventional care group, corresponding to a crude risk ratio of 0.55 (95% CI: 0.22-1.38). Mindfulness-based perioperative care was associated with improved objective and subjective sleep quality, more favorable autonomic and inflammatory biomarker profiles, better postoperative quality of life, and a lower observed rate of early atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence after radiofrequency catheter ablation for AF.

papers.title: Circadian and Sex-Specific Responses to Alternaria alternata in Allergic Airway Inflammation.
papers.abstract: Asthma severity and immune responses are regulated by circadian rhythms, yet the role of circadian timing in fungal allergen-induced airway inflammation remains poorly defined. Alternaria alternata , a clinically relevant fungal allergen, is strongly associated with severe asthma exacerbations and persistent airway dysfunction. Using a preclinical mouse model, we investigated whether pulmonary responses to Alternaria exposure are influenced by time of day and sex. We demonstrate that Alternaria induces allergic airway inflammation, airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR), and epithelial barrier disruption in a circadian- and sex-dependent manner. Female mice exhibited enhanced eosinophilic, neutrophilic, interstitial macrophage, and dendritic cell infiltration predominantly at Zeitgeber Time 0 (ZT0), whereas males showed stronger inflammatory responses at ZT12. Alternaria exposure increased IL-33 release and promoted ILC2 and Th2 cell accumulation, with distinct temporal patterns between sexes. Cytokine and chemokine profiling revealed robust Th2, proinflammatory, and Th17 responses that varied with exposure time, with higher responses at ZT12 in females and ZT0 in males. Markers of tissue injury, including lactate dehydrogenase and uric acid, followed similar circadian-dependent trends. Functionally, Alternaria -exposed mice displayed greater AHR during the resting phase, particularly in males. Additionally, Alternaria disrupted epithelial junctional proteins (E-cadherin and ZO-1) and altered expression of core circadian clock proteins CLOCK, BMAL1, and REV-ERBα. Mechanistically, peak inflammation coincided with enhanced STAT1, STAT3, and STAT6 activation. Collectively, these findings identify circadian timing and sex as key determinants of fungal allergen-induced airway inflammation and suggest chronotherapeutic approaches may improve asthma outcomes.

papers.title: Polysomnographic and nocturnal heart rate correlates of cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: To investigate the correlations between cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease (PD) and nocturnal video-polysomnography (vPSG) and electrocardiogram (ECG) parameters, evaluating their independent clinical value. We analyzed 84 PD patients divided into normal cognition (PD-NC, n = 27), mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI, n = 27), and dementia (PDD, n = 30) groups. Clinical scales, overnight vPSG, and electrocardiogram parameters were recorded. Multivariable linear regression was used to evaluate independent factors associated with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores. As cognitive impairment progressed, REM sleep latency significantly shortened (128.82 ± 117.32 min in PDD vs. 200.54 ± 90.26 min in PD-NC, p = 0.006). Concurrently, mean nocturnal heart rate (65.80 ± 10.80 bpm) and minimum heart rate (50.77 ± 12.51 bpm) were significantly higher in the PDD group than in the other two groups (p < 0.01). Multivariable linear regression revealed that, after adjusting for age, education, and UPDRS III score, mean nocturnal heart rate remained independently and negatively associated with MoCA scores (B = -0.158, β = -0.264, t = -3.018, p = 0.003), while REM sleep latency was independently and positively associated with MoCA scores (B = 0.010, β = 0.192, t = 2.224, p = 0.029). Collinearity diagnostics showed no significant multicollinearity (VIF: 1.029-1.261). Higher mean nocturnal heart rate and shorter REM sleep latency were independently associated with lower global cognitive performance in PD patients. Both measures can be obtained from routine overnight PSG, although their physiological significance remains uncertain. The cross-sectional design and the absence of direct autonomic or cholinergic measurements preclude causal or mechanistic conclusions.

papers.title: Non-Covalent Poly(ADP-ribose) Signaling Organizes a Circadian E3 Ligase Network in the Brain.
papers.abstract: Although PAR biology has traditionally been studied through covalent PARylation, non-covalent PAR-binding proteins provide an additional mechanism for interpreting transient PAR signals and converting them into downstream regulatory programs. Among these effectors, E3 ubiquitin ligases are uniquely positioned to couple PAR sensing to selective ubiquitination, thereby integrating stress signaling with proteostatic control. Because circadian systems depend heavily on temporally coordinated protein turnover, we hypothesized that PAR-binding E3 ligases may form a circadian-structured regulatory layer within the brain. To test this, we integrated GTEx v10 brain transcriptomics, GWAS Catalog gene-mapped associations, CIRCA circadian phase annotations, and Human Protein Atlas single-cell transcriptomic resources to characterize the organization of PAR-binding E3 ubiquitin ligases across neural tissues. Across the brain, the E3 ligase repertoire was broadly deployed yet regionally structured, with cerebellar and cortical enrichment patterns preserved within the PAR-binding subset. Representative ligases spanning circadian regulation, DNA repair, and neurodegeneration-relevant pathways displayed distinct abundance and regional-variability archetypes across GTEx brain regions. Human genetic analyses demonstrated that E3 ligases associated with cognition-, neurodegeneration-, and sleep/circadian-related phenotypes were disproportionately PAR-binding, supporting convergence between PAR-responsive ubiquitin regulation and disease-relevant biology. Circadian phase analyses further revealed that PAR-binding ligases occupy structured, non-random circadian windows within the broader E3 background, including distinct co-phasing relationships with BMAL1 and CRY1. Finally, cell-type enrichment analyses identified microglia as the dominant compartment for circadian-linked and PAR-binding circadian E3 weighting within the brain E3 program. Together, these findings support a systems-level framework in which non-covalent PAR-binding E3 ubiquitin ligases constitute a brain-deployed, circadian-organized regulatory layer that couples PAR signaling to time-dependent ubiquitin control in neural systems.

papers.title: Sex- and gender-related differences in narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Sex- and gender-related differences are increasingly recognised across central disorders of hypersomnolence, although evidence varies between narcolepsy type 1, narcolepsy type 2 and idiopathic hypersomnia. Literature suggests females experience longer diagnostic delays in narcolepsy and are more frequently diagnosed with idiopathic hypersomnia. Females also report greater subjective sleepiness, poorer quality of life and higher rates of psychiatric comorbidity, whereas males may experience greater impacts on personal relationships and higher rates of suicidality. Preclinical studies demonstrate sex-specific differences in the orexin system, stress responses, energy metabolism and neuroendocrine regulation, providing plausible mechanisms for clinical heterogeneity; however, human evidence remains limited and inconsistent. Sex-related differences in objective sleep testing and treatment response have been reported, although few studies were designed to evaluate these outcomes. Women face additional management challenges related to pregnancy, contraception and medication safety as reproductive safety data remain limited for many wake-promoting and anti-cataplectic therapies. Overall, substantial evidence gaps remain, particularly for narcolepsy type 2 and idiopathic hypersomnia. Future prospective, sex-stratified studies and objective biomarkers capable of identifying biologically meaningful disease subtypes are needed to improve diagnosis, refine disease classification and support personalised management.

papers.title: Chrononutrition, Dietary Patterns, and Sleep: A Narrative Review of Current Evidence and Practical Implications.
papers.abstract: Sleep and nutrition are closely interconnected through behavioral, metabolic, and circadian pathways, yet the strength of evidence varies considerably across dietary exposures. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on nutrients, foods, dietary patterns, chrononutrition, caffeine and alcohol in relation to sleep, while also considering the effects of insufficient sleep on dietary intake and metabolic health. The relevant literature was identified through searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science, supplemented by examination of reference lists and targeted searches. Higher-quality dietary patterns, particularly Mediterranean-style diets, are generally associated with more favorable sleep characteristics, although predominantly observational evidence limits causal interpretation. Intervention studies of individual foods and supplements have reported benefits for selected sleep outcomes, but findings remain heterogeneous and are often based on small samples. Evidence for meal timing and time-restricted eating is similarly inconsistent and does not support a single eating schedule for improving sleep. In contrast, caffeine and alcohol have relatively well-established sleep-disrupting effects. Insufficient sleep can also alter dietary intake, energy balance, glucose regulation, and adiposity, highlighting the bidirectional nature of these relationships. Nutritional approaches may complement broader strategies for sleep and health, but current evidence does not support specific foods, supplements, or eating schedules as stand-alone treatments for sleep problems.

papers.title: Multimodal evidence associated with 20Hz rTMS in AD: neuroaxonal injury reduction, neural oscillatory rebalancing, and multilayer network integration.
papers.abstract: High-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been demonstrated to enhance cognitive function in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the neurobiological mechanisms associated with neuroaxonal injury, neural oscillatory dynamics, and large-scale network reorganization remain unclear. In this study, we first conducted a randomized, sham-controlled trial with 16 patients with AD to evaluate the efficacy of DLPFC-targeted rTMS, followed by a single-arm multimodal cohort study of 30 patients to explore potential neurobiological mechanisms through cognitive assessments, blood biomarkers, EEG oscillatory activity, and multiplex brain network analysis. In Stage 1, the sham group showed no significant pre-post changes in MMSE or MoCA scores (MMSE: Z = -0.738, Cohen's r = 0.26; MoCA: Z =-0.853, Cohen's r = 0.30). The active rTMS group showed improvements in MMSE (Z = -2.124, Cohen's r = 0.75) and MoCA (Z = -2.108, Cohen's r = 0.75). In stage 2, rTMS was associated with improvements in MMSE (Z = -2.863, Cohen's r = 0.523) and MoCA (t = -6.137, Cohen's r = 0.752) scores. Biomarker analyses indicated a significant decrease in NfL concentrations (Z=-2.371, Cohen's r=0.484). EEG recordings revealed a decrease in delta power in the left temporal lobe (t=2.158, Cohen's r=0.372) and increases in beta power in the right parietal lobe and gamma power in the temporal lobe (beta: Z=-2.088, Cohen's r=0.381; gamma: Z=-2.129, Cohen's r=0.389). papers.title: Temporal evolution of EEG hallmarks in childhood Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.
papers.abstract: The temporal development of generalized paroxysmal fast activity (GPFA) and slow spike-and-wave complexes in childhood Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS) remains poorly characterized. This study mapped the emergence and longitudinal evolution of these EEG hallmarks in a real-world LGS cohort. This retrospective observational cohort study was conducted at a tertiary pediatric neurophysiology and neurology center. Patients aged 1-18 years fulfilling current International League Against Epilepsy criteria for LGS were identified through local databases. All available sleep video-EEG recordings before November 2024 were reviewed; clinical features, EEG findings, and comorbidities were collected at each recording. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. We reviewed 234 EEGs from 51 patients (75% male). Median age at first EEG was 5 years. GPFA emerged later than slow spike-and-wave (mean age: 9.6 vs 8.3 years, p = 0.002), with non-parametric analysis confirming a significant difference in age at first detection (p = 0.004). Median age at epilepsy onset was 1.1 years, while all clinical and EEG criteria for LGS were met at a median age of 10.9 years. EEG hallmarks of LGS emerged progressively during childhood, with slow spike-and-wave preceding GPFA during sleep. Following early clinical manifestations, a prolonged developmental phase may precede full electroclinical expression of LGS, with implications for early diagnosis and longitudinal EEG surveillance.

papers.title: The Circadian Clock in Glioblastoma: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential.
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive brain cancer in adults. Circadian rhythms regulate the sleep-wake cycle, which influences the body's physiological functions. Disruption of circadian rhythms is associated with certain neurological diseases, including GBM. The present narrative review highlights the relationship between circadian rhythm and GBM, the related mechanisms, and the therapeutic approaches against GBM. It also discusses how alterations in the expression of core circadian genes contribute to glioma genesis, especially GBM, and how restoring normal circadian gene function may suppress GBM progression. Additionally, chronotherapy could be considered a potential therapeutic approach for GBM. Aligning chemotherapy and radiotherapy with the internal clock of each patient may have the potential to increase the efficacy of treatments. A better understanding of the potential mechanisms underlying the association between circadian rhythm and GBM pathogenesis may help guide future circadian-based therapeutic approaches; however, further investigation is required.

papers.title: Mapping Retinal Gene Expression to Cell Classes: Insights into Retinal Circadian Rhythms.
papers.abstract: Many retinal processes are regulated by circadian rhythms. Previous studies have identified genes with rhythmic retinal expression over a 24 h cycle, but the cell class specificity of many of these genes remains unknown. Here we present a mathematical model, based on existing human retinal single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data and validated using known retinal markers, which assigns cell classes to genes showing uniquely enriched expression in that class. This model assigns retinal cell class specificity to over 10,000 human genes and provides potential novel candidates for retinal cell markers. Additionally, the model enables transcriptomic datasets to be investigated through cell class enrichment analysis. We apply this model to circadian-expressed genes from published mouse ocular transcriptomic data. Specific cell classes were assigned to over 35% of these genes, many of which have little to no previous literature denoting their retinal localisation and role. We also demonstrate significant enrichment of photoreceptor-associated transcripts, many of which are associated with phototransduction and outer segment turnover. The methods and data presented here provide a resource for researchers interested in the cell class specific expression of retinal genes and provide new insight into the cellular basis of retinal circadian rhythms.

papers.title: A melatonin textile transdermal patch based on physicochemical synergistic permeation-enhancement strategy for circadian rhythm regulation.
papers.abstract: Melatonin, an endogenous circadian rhythm-regulating hormone, has faced challenges in achieving prolonged exogenous regulation due to its low oral bioavailability and short half-life. Existing transdermal strategies are difficult to balance efficacy, safety, and accessibility. To address this, we propose a physicochemical synergistic permeation-enhancement strategy and have developed a melatonin textile transdermal patch based on the synergistic action of electret and permeation enhancer. The patch is designed with a three-layer composite structure, composed of a textile-based electret backing layer, a drug-loading pressure sensitive adhesive layer containing melatonin and permeation enhancer, and a protective layer to prevent drug leakage. Electret and permeation enhancer enhance transdermal efficiency through a physicochemical synergistic permeation-enhancement strategy without disrupting the skin barrier. In vitro studies revealed that among various permeation enhancers (menthol, azone, oleic acid) and electret parameters, the combination of a -1500 V electret with 10% oleic acid exhibited the optimal synergistic effect. In vivo pharmacokinetic studies demonstrated that the patch reached a peak plasma concentration (>30 ng/mL) within 1 h and maintained effective therapeutic levels (>5 ng/mL) for up to 8 h. The patch significantly improved the sleep quality in insomniac rats, with no observed skin irritation or cytotoxicity. This study not only accomplishes an efficient, non-invasive, and parametrically tunable transdermal delivery of melatonin but also validates the feasibility of synergistic enhancement through physical field regulation and chemical permeation, thereby providing a viable strategy for developing safe and long-acting textile-based transdermal drug delivery systems aimed at neuroendocrine small-molecule hormones similar to melatonin.

papers.title: Nanoscale remodeling of synaptic glutamate receptors and calcium channels in temporal lobe epilepsy
papers.abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is the most common form of focal epilepsy and remains drug-resistant in approximately one-third of patients, for whom surgical resection of the epileptogenic zone is currently the most effective treatment option. One strategy to improve therapeutic outcomes involves identifying the molecular mechanisms and key regulators underlying synaptic function. Although altered glutamatergic neurotransmission is considered a major contributor to epileptic hyperexcitability, the nanoscale organization of key synaptic proteins in the human epileptic cortex is still not well characterized. In particular, it remains unclear whether pre- and postsynaptic proteins undergo synapse-type-specific remodeling in TLE. Here, we used high-resolution freeze-fracture replica immunolabeling to map the nanoscale organization of postsynaptic AMPA receptors (AMPARs) and presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (CaV2.1) in glutamatergic synapses of cortical layers II/III of surgically resected human tissue. We examined perilesional, cytologically unremarkable, non-epileptogenic cortical tissue obtained from patients undergoing tumor resection (52-63 years; two female and three male patients) and compared these data with cortical samples from patients with refractory TLE (22-53 years; two female and four male patients). To assess whether pathological remodeling differs across synapse populations, we analyzed both excitatory dendritic spine and shaft synapses. We found a robust, highly consistent increase in AMPAR density at both spine and shaft synapses in TLE patients indicating enhanced postsynaptic excitatory signaling. However, AMPAR spatial reorganization differed between synapse types. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated that spine synapses largely preserved a random receptor distribution without a significant clustering pattern, whereas shaft synapses exhibited a redistribution from clustering toward random receptor arrangements together with reduced center-preference within the postsynaptic density. In contrast, presynaptic CaV2.1 remodeling was more variable and predominantly associated with excitatory spine synapses. TLE spine synapses exhibited an overall increase in CaV2.1 density together with significantly larger and more numerous CaV2.1 nanoclusters within the active zone. This difference was particularly pronounced in male patients. In comparison, shaft synapses displayed only minor presynaptic alterations. CaV2.1 channels remained highly clustered under both control and epileptic conditions, indicating preservation of core active-zone organizational features despite disease-associated nanoscale remodeling. Together, these findings provide direct ultrastructural support that pathological plasticity in human TLE involves an overall increase in excitatory postsynaptic responsiveness and a target cell-specific increase of excitatory release probability at cortical synapses.

papers.title: Recognizing fibromyalgia-like pain phenotypes in lipedema: A narrative review.
papers.abstract: IntroductionLipedema is a chronic adipose and connective tissue disorder in which pain is classically localized to affected limb tissue. However, some patients report joint, periarticular, myotendinous, or axial pain, with fatigue, sleep disturbance, and exercise intolerance. When symptoms become widespread, the presentation may resemble fibromyalgia (FM), creating a diagnostic challenge for phlebologists.ObjectivesTo provide a clinical framework for distinguishing characteristic lipedema tissue pain from musculoskeletal pain generators, secondary central pain amplification, and potentially coexisting FM.MethodsThis narrative review was conducted with reference to the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA). PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched through May 2026 for studies addressing lipedema, FM, widespread pain, hypermobility, connective tissue vulnerability, biomechanical dysfunction, and pain sensitization. Reference lists were manually screened. No formal risk-of-bias assessment or quantitative synthesis was performed.ResultsCharacteristic lipedema pain is predominantly localized to affected adipose tissue and associated with tenderness, pressure sensitivity, easy bruising, and functional impairment. Observational studies have also reported joint and periarticular pain, axial symptoms, hypermobility, and biomechanical dysfunction in patient subsets. Extra-adipose pain should be assessed separately and not automatically attributed either to lipedema or independent FM. Tissue hypersensitivity, stromal and microvascular alterations, joint instability, and altered biomechanics may represent peripheral pain generators contributing to secondary central amplification. However, observational evidence does not establish whether widespread pain is intrinsic to lipedema, secondary to musculoskeletal dysfunction or central amplification, or reflects coexisting FM.ConclusionsIn patients with lipedema and extra-adipose or widespread pain, phlebologists should assess joint hypermobility, instability, biomechanical dysfunction, and axial or musculoskeletal pain. FM criteria identify a widespread pain phenotype but cannot determine whether it represents an independent comorbidity or is related to persistent peripheral nociceptive mechanisms. Multidisciplinary assessment may improve diagnostic characterization and individualized management.

papers.title: Cofactors in Anaphylaxis: Insights From the European Anaphylaxis Registry.
papers.abstract: The role of cofactors contributing to anaphylaxis severity remains unclear. We analysed data from the European Anaphylaxis Registry (2007-2024) to determine the impact of suspected cofactors on reaction severity. Adjusted odds ratios (aOR) were calculated for the number of organ systems affected, but also two severity classification systems (Ring/Messmer and Brown). At least one suspected cofactor was reported in 8310 cases (49%) out of 16,915. Cofactors were less frequently suspected among younger patients (< 18 years: 26% and ≥ 18 years: 59%). Medication was the most common suspected cofactor in adults (41%), followed by exercise (27%), which was in parallel the most frequent suspected cofactor in children (19%). Emotional burden (children 3%/adults 8%), alcohol (0.4%/8%), sleep deprivation (0.5%/2%) and menstruation (2%/4%) were less commonly reported. We observed a trend between reaction severity and an increasing number of suspected cofactors. Among suspected cofactors, we observed consistent effects on anaphylaxis reaction severity for acute infections among children and alcohol consumption among adults in food-induced reactions. Moreover, we identified an association between the presence of a suspected cofactor(s) and an increased time interval between exposure and onset of symptoms across all age groups in food-induced anaphylaxis. Our data suggest an age-dependent role of suspected cofactors in anaphylaxis severity. Clinicians should explore the presence of cofactors in patients who experienced anaphylaxis, in particular in those with prolonged time intervals between exposure and reaction onset.

papers.title: Parathyroid Storm Secondary to a Parathyroid Adenoma Presenting With Recurrent Generalised Tonic-Clonic Seizures and Refractory Hypercalcaemia: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Parathyroid storm is a rare, life-threatening manifestation of primary hyperparathyroidism characterised by severe hypercalcaemia and acute multisystem deterioration. We report a 70-year-old woman with known primary hyperparathyroidism who presented with progressive weakness, confusion and reduced mobility and was found to have a corrected serum calcium concentration of 4.14 mmol/L. Despite aggressive intravenous hydration, she developed recurrent generalised tonic-clonic seizures, hypoventilation and reduced consciousness, requiring intubation and intensive care admission. Electroencephalography demonstrated severe diffuse cerebral dysfunction consistent with metabolic encephalopathy, while cerebrospinal fluid studies were unremarkable. Four-dimensional computed tomography of the neck identified a 1.8 cm right-sided parathyroid lesion. Hypercalcaemia remained difficult to control despite multimodal medical therapy, including pamidronate, calcitonin, cinacalcet and denosumab, with recurrent rebound hypercalcaemia. Urgent parathyroidectomy resulted in sustained normalisation of serum calcium and cessation of seizure activity, and histopathology confirmed a benign parathyroid adenoma. This case highlights the severe neurological complications of parathyroid storm and the importance of early multidisciplinary consideration of definitive surgery when hypercalcaemia remains refractory to intensive medical therapy.

papers.title: Interpreting Cytomegalovirus Seropositivity Beyond the Neonatal Diagnostic Window: A Case Report on an Infant With Early-Onset Atopic Dermatitis and Congenital Arthrogryposis.
papers.abstract: Congenital cytomegalovirus (cCMV) infection has a broad clinical spectrum and may result in permanent neurological, auditory, visual, and developmental sequelae. We report the case of a six-month-old male infant investigated primarily for microcephaly who had a complex phenotype comprising a cutaneous rash present from birth that evolved into moderate early-onset atopic dermatitis with severe clinical and quality-of-life impairment, growth impairment, congenital arthrogryposis, neonatal jaundice with hyperbilirubinemia, mild neonatal thrombocytopenia, and neurosensory abnormalities. He was born at 36 weeks and four days after reduced amniotic fluid volume was noted at approximately 36 weeks. Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia did not require phototherapy, and a follow-up peripheral blood smear was unremarkable. At six months, the dermatitis consisted of widespread erythematous-squamous, intensely pruritic lesions with facial and periorbital involvement and sleep disturbance. After 40 days of conventional treatment with emollients, skin-barrier care, and topical corticosteroids, the SCORAD (Scoring Atopic Dermatitis) index decreased from 45 to 18, although residual lesions persisted. Growth was impaired, with marked underweight (weight-for-age z-score <-3) and reduced linear growth (length-for-age z-score -2.6), while head circumference was 40.8 cm (z-score -2.2), consistent with microcephaly. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed preserved cerebral architecture with symmetric periventricular and peritrigonal T2 hyperintensity considered indeterminate and potentially related to incomplete physiological myelination. Auditory brainstem evoked responses and visual evoked potentials were abnormal. Creatine kinase was mildly elevated, whereas neurological examination and electromyography were normal. Quantitative immunoglobulins, serum protein electrophoresis, and lymphocyte subset analysis were unremarkable. Maternal CMV-specific IgM and IgG were positive during the eighth month of pregnancy, and the infant had positive CMV-specific IgM and IgG at six months. In the absence of virological testing within the first 21 days of life or an archived neonatal dried blood spot, congenital infection could not be definitively confirmed. This case emphasizes the critical importance of recognizing suggestive neonatal findings and testing for cCMV within the first 21 days of life, particularly in settings where retrospective dried-blood-spot testing is unavailable.

papers.title: Creative patient and public engagement to amplify the voices of people living with eczema.
papers.abstract: Qualitative research has captured human experiences of suffering associated with atopic eczema. We aimed to convey this information beyond academic manuscripts to a broader audience, using ambitious, multidisciplinary patient and public engagement, led by creative researchers. We worked with patient communities to find ways to amplify eczema voices, using previously reported and newly collected quotes describing their experiences. The resulting "Surface Echoes" project combined audio and visual methods, developed by a collaborative team of creatives, working with stakeholder participants. A script for reading aloud in small groups, and a digital audio recording were created through a process of collaging the collected quotes, curated by the patient communities, creatives and researchers. Themes presented in this work include visual appearance and mental burden of embarrassment or shame (" it's a kind of social handicap…"); pain and itch; lack of clarity around treatment (" I think this 'trial and error' is a very primitive form of medicine"); challenges of communicating with healthcare professionals; and the morbidity associated with sleep deprivation (" It's impossible to be on sick leave just because you are tired. So I carried on throughout the Spring and then I completely collapsed"). The curated quotes also report positive healthcare experiences, indicative of good practice: " I felt listened to … it was a conversation". Project participants used creative research methods to develop imaginaries of better futures, for example, " … sunshine soup" and "… consistent advice". The materials have been used with stakeholders including medical and nursing professionals, industrial and academic researchers, and the public. This work has been designed to raise awareness, promote discussion, reduce stigma and increase understanding of eczema. The presentation to stakeholder groups prioritised by the participants whose voices are amplified was designed to improve empathic discussion with professionals; it may also inform future research.
